analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and agencies to tell people when their personal data has been stolen, and lets regulators fine those that fail to.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the House and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The CARD Act of 2005 would have required any government agency or company doing interstate business to notify people when a data breach exposed their personal information — a name tied to a Social Security number, driver's license number, or account number. Notices would have to describe what was taken and give a toll-free number and the credit bureaus' contact details. It would have let the Federal Trade Commission fine companies up to $1,000 per affected person or $50,000 per day of delay, let breach victims sue, let state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf, and made it easier for consumers to place an extended fraud alert on their credit file after a breach notice. It also said its provisions would override conflicting state and local laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose personal or financial information is exposed in a data breach would learn about it without unreasonable delay, with a toll-free number to check whether their data was held and the credit bureaus' contact information included in the notice. Anyone notified that their financial information was compromised could get an extended fraud alert on their credit file without first filing an identity theft report. People injured by a covered violation could sue for damages, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents to force compliance and recover restitution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose personal data is breached

how_it_helps.text: Any agency or business in interstate commerce that holds personal information — a name paired with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or account/card number — would have to tell each affected person when that data was, or was likely, taken by an unauthorized person.

Notices would have to say what kinds of data were taken, include a toll-free number consumers could call to find out what information the company held on them, and list the contact numbers for the major credit reporting agencies.

It would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that a consumer who shows they received notice that their financial information was compromised can get an extended fraud alert placed in their credit file — currently that alert generally requires an identity theft report.

The FTC could fine violators up to $1,000 per affected person or $50,000 per day of delay, victims could sue for damages, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents to force compliance and win restitution.
Companies would bear the burden of proving their notifications were timely, and delays had to be justified in writing, including law-enforcement delay requests.

analysis.who_pays: Any business or agency holding consumer personal information would bear the cost of detecting breaches, notifying affected individuals (with the burden of proving timeliness), and potential fines of up to $1,000 per person or $50,000 per day of delay, plus damages in civil suits. Because the bill preempts inconsistent state law, state attorneys general would also have lost the ability to enforce stricter state notification rules where this federal standard was weaker.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies and agencies holding personal data

drawbacks.text: Section 5 supersedes 'any inconsistent provisions of law of any State or unit of local government,' meaning a federal floor could have preempted stricter state breach-notification laws, such as state rules requiring faster or broader disclosure than this bill requires.

Companies could delay notifying victims while they 'determine the scope of the breach' and restore their systems, and they could use cheaper 'substitute notice' — a website posting and media alerts — instead of contacting individuals directly whenever more than 500,000 people were affected or direct notice cost over $500,000.

Law enforcement could put notification on hold with a written request, and heads of agencies could exempt themselves by certifying national-security or law-enforcement harm — checks and paperwork limits, but still discretionary exceptions in a bill about telling people their data was taken.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and would have cost little for consumers: people whose Social Security or card numbers are stolen would find out quickly, with a toll-free number to check what data was held on them and a path to a fraud alert, and fines up to $1,000 per affected person plus state attorney general suits give companies a reason to secure data. The main cost falls on businesses holding data, which is the point. The bill's serious design weakness is its preemption clause: a national law that supersedes inconsistent state rules could have replaced stronger state breach laws and, because Congress produced no competing national standard, consumers could have ended up with the weaker federal floor instead of tougher local rules. On balance a modest, soundly aimed consumer bill that carried one avoidable trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress and expired without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 2005 and referred the same day to three House committees: Energy and Commerce, Government Reform, and Financial Services.

In early August 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection and to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House, and no Senate companion action is recorded; it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses holding personal data are better off: no federal duty to disclose breaches, no fines, and no private right of action was created. Consumers lost a notification right and an easier path to fraud alerts.

for.name: Rep. Julia Carson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 28, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks in the House on July 29, 2005.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referring it to its Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection Subcommittee on August 5, 2005.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referring it to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee on August 24, 2005.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after the original three-way referral on July 28, 2005.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member was ever attached to the bill — its Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party — so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.industry: Data brokers and any business holding customer personal data
industries.note: The bill would have required them to tell customers when personal data was compromised, with civil fines up to $1,000 per person and exposure to private lawsuits and state attorney general actions. Ordinary people whose data is stolen would learn of it sooner and could act faster.

Companies reporting breaches affecting more than 1,000 people would have to coordinate with the nationwide credit bureaus, and breach notices would direct consumers to the bureaus' phone numbers. The bill also eases access to extended fraud alerts, a bureau-administered protection. Their gatekeeping role over consumers' credit files stays in place and is reinforced.
